1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163	
164	## Finish
165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractChronic urticaria is a common condition characterized by recurrent hives lasting several weeks or months and is usually idiopathic. Approximately half of the individuals with chronic urticaria will present with episodes of angioedema that can be severe and debilitating. In this report, we describe a 47-year-old Hispanic male who presented initially for an evaluation of chronic hives following hospitalization due to hive-induced anaphylaxis. The individual had a history significant for urticaria and angioedema beginning in his early 30s. Interestingly, both the individual's 41-year-old sister and 12-year-old daughter were also affected with chronic urticaria and severe angioedema. Whole exome sequencing of the proband and several family members revealed a heterozygous variant of uncertain significance in exon 2 ofTNFAIP3, denoted as c.65G>A (p.R22Q), in all affected members. Variants inTNFAIP3 have been associated with multiple autoimmune diseases, susceptibility to allergy and asthma, and periodic fever syndromes, suggesting that this variant could potentially play a role in disease.

14	## 1. Introduction
15	
16	Chronic urticaria is a common skin disorder characterized by recurrent hives lasting more than six weeks or hives that recur over several months or years [1, 2]. It is mainly a disease of adults with women being more affected than men [3]. Chronic urticaria is usually idiopathic, arising spontaneously without a stimulus. Other common types include physical urticarias that are caused by physical stimuli such as cold, heat, or pressure. Various types of urticaria may coexist together, which is not uncommon [3]. Angioedema is a swelling of the deeper epidermal and dermal layers of the skin. The association between chronic urticaria and angioedema is well established [4, 5]. Genetic factors may play a role in chronic idiopathic urticaria, but the mechanism of disease is largely unknown [6]. In this report, we describe a patient with a several-year history of chronic hives, angioedema, skin flushing, and swelling. Whole exome sequencing (WES) did not detect any causative variants in known disease genes but did identify a variant in tumor necrosis factor-alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3, known commonly as A20) that is possibly associated with the reported phenotype.
17	
18	## 2. Case History
19	
20	A 47-year-old Hispanic male was initially referred to the Mayo Clinic at 34 years of age due to severe episodes of angioedema (occurring every three to four months) and history of chronic urticaria. The initial onset of urticaria occurred in 2002 while the proband was living in Italy. He has since relocated to the United States, where he sought treatment for his urticaria flares. The proband reported that episodes of urticaria occur when his skin is exposed to hot or cold temperatures or significant pressure.
21	
22	The proband tried numerous treatment modalities to suppress his urticaria, including the following antihistamines: levocetirizine, cetirizine, fexofenadine, and loratadine. Prednisone and steroid injections were the only treatments that cleared the patient's hives; however, treatment with prednisone was eventually stopped due to side effects. His elevated levels of IgE suggested that the hives were autoimmune in nature, though the accompanying tryptase elevation led to the consideration of mastocytosis. The patient had a normal bone marrow biopsy (differential and aspirate), a complete blood count (CBC) with differential within normal limits, and a normal mast cell panel (CD2, CD25, CD69, and CD117). His anti-IgE receptor antibody was elevated at 18.5% (reference range: <13%) and his C1q complement was elevated at 43 (12–22 mg/dL). He also had a normal TSH of 2.0 (>20 years: 0.3–4.2 mIU/L) and serum protein electrophoresis that was within normal limits. His tryptase levels were consistently elevated and ranged from 13.9 and 19.2 (<11.5 ng/mL), indicating mast cell activation. Due to the absence of mast cells in the bone marrow biopsy, the patient did not meet diagnostic criteria for mastocytosis and was ultimately diagnosed with chronic urticaria. At 37 years of age, the patient began experiencing “attacks” approximately every two weeks, which he described as involving hives, fever, weakness, diaphoresis, and diarrhea. The patient also experienced episodes of dizziness when standing after walking only a few feet.

24	Upon ascertainment of family history, we found that one of the proband's sisters and his daughter both shared his symptoms of hives and angioedema (Figure 1). 28	## 3. Methods
29	
30	### 3.1. Whole Exome Sequencing
31	
32	Using genomic DNA extracted from the proband, his mother, sister, and daughter, the Agilent Clinical Research Exome kit was used to target exonic regions and flanking splice junctions of the genome. These regions were sequenced by massively parallel sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq with 100 bp paired-end reads (mean depth of coverage: 119x; quality threshold: 94.9%). Bidirectional sequence was assembled, aligned to reference gene sequences based on human genome build GRCh37/UCSC hg19, and analyzed for sequence variants using a custom-developed analysis tool (Xome Analyzer, GeneDx). Capillary sequencing was used to confirm the presence or absence of all potentially pathogenic variants identified in both the proband and relative samples.
33	
34	### 3.2. Structural Modeling
35	
36	TNFAIP3, also known as A20, is an ubiquitin-editing enzyme, which has dual roles in ubiquitin ligase and deubiquitinase activity. The N-terminal domain of TNFAIP3 contains an ovarian tumor (OTU) domain, involved in deubiquitinating Lys-63-polyubiquitin chains in a number of substrates. The C-terminal domain of TNFAIP3 is composed of seven zinc finger domains that coordinate ubiquitin ligase activity, including the addition of lysine-48-linked ubiquitin chains that are necessary for targeting substrates for proteasomal degradation [7, 8].
37	
38	Human TNFAIP3 sequence was taken from the NCBI Reference Accession number NG_032761 version NG_032761.1 and was used for computer-assisted modeling. Monte Carlo simulations were performed on the full-length wild type protein (791 amino acids) and the p.R22Q variant. The X-ray refinement for Monte Carlo was built using YASARA SSP/PSSM method [9–14]. The structure was relaxed to the YASARA/Amber force field using knowledge-based potentials within YASARA. The side chains and rotamers were adjusted with knowledge-based potentials, simulated annealing with explicit solvent, and small equilibration simulations using YASARA's refinement protocol [15]. The entire full-length structure was modeled, filling in any gaps or unresolved portions from the X-ray.
39	
40	Refinement of the finalized models was completed using either Schrodinger's LC-MOD Monte Carlo-based module or NAMD2 protocols. These refinements started with YASARA generated initial refinement [9–11, 13]. The superposition and subsequent refinement of the overlapping regions yielded a complete model for TNFAIP3. The final structures were subjected to energy optimization with PR conjugate gradient with an R-dependent dielectric.
41	
42	Atom consistency was checked for all 791 amino acids (13,028 atoms) of the full-length wild type model and 791 amino acids (13,028 atoms) for the p.R22Q variant, verifying correctness of chain name, dihedrals, angles, torsions, nonbonds, electrostatics, atom typing, and parameters. Each model was exported to the following formats: Maestro (MAE) and YASARA (PDB). Model manipulation was done with Maestro (Macromodel, version 9.8, Schrodinger, LLC, New York, NY, 2010) or Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) [16]. Analyses were restricted to the N-terminus region containing the first 350 amino acids given the length and C-term distance from the site of mutation.
43	
44	Monte Carlo dynamics searching (LCMOD-MC) was completed on each model for conformational sampling, using methods previously described in the literature [17–20]. Briefly, each TNFAIP3 variant system was minimized with relaxed restraints using either Steepest Descent or Conjugate Gradient PR and then allowed to undergo the MC search criteria, as shown in the literature [17–20]. The primary purpose of MC, in this scenario, is to examine any conformational variability that may occur with different mutations in the region near the mutation and the possible effect on TNFAIP3 structure and function.

46	## 4. Results
47	
48	### 4.1. Exome Sequencing Results
49	
50	WES of the proband uncovered a novel variant inTNFAIP3 (Chr6(GRCh38): g.137871292G>A; NM_001270507.1: c.65G>A; p.(Arg22Gln)), which could possibly correlate with the proband's disease phenotype. The p.R22Q variant is absent from ExAC (Exome Aggregation Consortium) and has only been observed in 1/30936 whole genomes sequenced in gnomAD (Genome Aggregation Database) [21]. Of note, this variant was seen in 1/838 Latino genomes with a predicted minor allele frequency (MAF) of 0.001193%, suggesting that it may be more common in Latino populations. The Arg22 residue is conserved across species down to zebrafish(Danio rerio), andin silico prediction algorithms predict the variant to be deleterious (PredictSNP2 deleterious score: 1.0000; CADD deleterious score: 22.6000; FATHMM deleterious score: 0.9806) [22]. This variant results in a semiconservative amino acid substitution that may impact secondary protein structure, and more detailed studies includingin silico molecular modeling and dynamics simulations were pursued. Based on the ACMG 2015 guidelines, the c.65G>A (p.R22Q) variant was classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) [23]. The proband's mother was found to be negative for the p.R22Q variant (the proband's father was deceased), whereas both his daughter and sister (both affected) were heterozygous for the VUS. Another pathogenic variant was detected inGJB2 (Chr13(GRCh38): g.20189547del; NM_004004.5: c.35del; p.Gly12Valfs∗2; exon 2) in the proband and his mother only, which may be associated with his mild hearing loss.
51	
52	### 4.2. Structure-Function Results
53	
54	When comparing the wild type and the p.R22Q variant, we found the energetic stability of the object based on ΔG per amino acid calculations to be comparable. The wild type object stability was 53.12 kcal/mol∗Å^2, while the p.R22Q variant results in a net increase in free energy of 0.755 kcal/aa∗mol∗Å^2, which could be locally destabilizing [17–19, 24–27]. This object stability was positive, indicating that some dynamic changes are likely with a molecular simulation for conformational sampling. Thus, we examined the local residues and determined that an electrostatic calculation may be useful to explain the change in function. The molecular models for the full structure and its variant form were generated (Figure 2) using previously described methods [17–20, 24, 27–34].

66	## 5. Conclusion
67	
68	This report describes a 47-year-old Hispanic male with an extensive history of chronic urticaria and angioedema that various treatment modalities failed to resolve. It was initially suggested that the patient might have mastocytosis or autoimmune-related hives due to his elevated tryptase and IgE levels, respectively. Bone marrow biopsy and computerized tomography (CT) scans ruled out visceral involvement by systemic mastocytosis, and the patient was later diagnosed with chronic urticaria. The cause of his chronic urticaria is unknown; however, a history of hives in the proband's daughter and sister led to genetic testing of some of his family members. Two genes were identified through WES:TNFAIP3 andGJB2.
69	
70	The c.35delG variant inGJB2has been reported previously in association with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss when present in the homozygous state or when intrans with another pathogenic variant [35]. This variant is the most commonGJB2pathogenic variant among individuals of European ancestry, and the hearing loss present in individuals homozygous for the c.35delG variant ranges from mild to profound [36]. Most individuals known to be heterozygous for this variant have normal hearing, although subclinical differences in the otoacoustic emissions of carriers have been noted upon audiologic examination [37]. The proband's mother was heterozygous for the c.35delG variant inGJB2while his sister and daughter did not carry this variant.
71	
72	The proband, his daughter, and his sister who are all affected with chronic urticaria and angioedema each carry the c.65G>A (p.R22Q) variant inTNFAIP3. The variant is absent in the proband's mother who is unaffected. This variant inTNFAIP3 has not been reported previously as pathogenic or benign to our knowledge and was classified as a VUS. However,TNFAIP3 is known to be involved in immune and inflammatory responses signaled by cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-1 beta [38]. Additionally, multiple variants within the gene have been associated with autoimmune diseases, susceptibility to allergy and asthma, and periodic fever syndromes [39].
73	
74	TNFAIP3 is a ubiquitin-editing enzyme that participates in ubiquitin ligase and deubiquitinase activities. It is also known to have multiple overlapping functions between nuclear factor kappa B (NFκB) and interferon regulatory factors (IRF) [8, 40]. There is evidence of cross talk between these two signaling pathways and their roles in the inflammatory and antiviral responses, which positions TNFAIP3 as a key effector of the innate immune response [41]. Recently, Zhou et al. (2016) identified individuals from six different families affected with a Behçet-like autoinflammatory syndrome (MIM: 616744) that has a variable presentation including uveitis, chorioretinal scarring, oral, gastrointestinal, and genital ulcers, gastrointestinal inflammation, polyarthritis, rash, periodic fevers, and autoinflammation with the production of autoantibodies and increased circulating proinflammatory cytokines [42]. The age of onset for this disorder is usually in the first or second decade; however, only a few cases have been reported to date.
75	
76	Currently, there is no known association between missense variants inTNFAIP3 and familial chronic urticaria with angioedema. Many patients with chronic urticaria improve with anti-IgE therapy (omalizumab), suggesting that inappropriate activation of mast cells and basophils may play a role in disease pathogenesis. It has also been proposed that some individuals with chronic urticaria may produce IgE directed against self-antigens, but evidence for this has been lacking. The proband in this study had elevated tryptase and IgE levels, suggesting that he may benefit from a trial of this therapy in the future. Interestingly, TNFAIP3 has been shown to regulate inflammation downstream of the mast cell antigen receptor module as well as the alarmin receptor, IL-33R [43]. Heger et al. (2014) showed that mast cell-specific ablation ofTnfaip3 in mice exacerbated disease in mouse models for rheumatoid arthritis and asthma, suggesting that dysregulation of mast cell inflammatory responses via Tnfaip3 loss can contribute to disease pathology [43].
77	
78	In summary, we report a novel variant inTNFAIP3in three family members, which potentially correlates with a phenotype of chronic urticaria. Additional studies, including functional analyses, will be necessary to determine the role ofTNFAIP3variation in susceptibility to chronic urticaria.
